questions.q: What does a CIS Benchmark provide, according to this lesson?
options: A marketing comparison of cloud providers
A vendor-neutral list of vague best-practice statements with no audit procedure
A numbered list of specific, testable recommendations, each with rationale, audit procedure, and remediation steps
A single universal checklist identical across every cloud provider
questions.explain: CIS Benchmarks give concrete, testable recommendations (not vague advice), each with a rationale, an audit procedure to check current state, and remediation steps.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between a Level 1 and a Level 2 CIS recommendation?
options: Level 1 only applies to AWS; Level 2 only applies to Azure
Level 1 recommendations have minimal operational tradeoff and are adopted broadly; Level 2 recommendations introduce real tradeoffs and are adopted deliberately based on risk tolerance
There is no practical difference; the levels are purely cosmetic labels
Level 2 recommendations are optional suggestions with no audit procedure at all
questions.explain: Level 1 is baseline, low-impact configuration that nearly every organization adopts; Level 2 goes further into defense-in-depth with real operational tradeoffs, adopted based on actual risk tolerance.

questions.q: In the Azure example recommendation discussed in this lesson (requiring MFA for privileged users), what does the audit procedure involve?
options: Checking Entra ID security defaults or Conditional Access policies to confirm MFA is required for privileged roles
Reviewing AWS CloudTrail logs for root account activity
Running a Terraform plan against the subscription
Checking the Azure billing portal for license tier
questions.explain: The audit procedure for this recommendation concretely checks Entra ID's security defaults or Conditional Access configuration for MFA enforcement on privileged roles.

questions.q: How does Microsoft Defender for Cloud make use of the CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark?
options: It ignores CIS Benchmarks entirely in favor of a proprietary standard
It requires the benchmark to be manually re-checked once per year
It only supports the AWS CIS Benchmark, not the Azure one
It ships the benchmark as a built-in regulatory compliance standard, continuously scoring the environment's pass/fail against each applicable recommendation
questions.explain: Defender for Cloud includes the CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark as a built-in regulatory compliance standard, reflecting real-time compliance in the secure score.

questions.q: What is the role of Azure Policy or AWS Config rules in relation to a CIS baseline, per this lesson?
options: They are unrelated to CIS Benchmarks and serve only cost-management purposes
They proactively enforce specific recommendations, such as denying creation of a storage account without HTTPS-only enforced, rather than just flagging violations after the fact
They only generate billing alerts, not security enforcement
They replace the need for Microsoft Defender for Cloud or AWS Security Hub entirely
questions.explain: Azure Policy and AWS Config rules provide proactive enforcement of CIS recommendations, preventing non-compliant resources from being created rather than only detecting them afterward.
